Sanction

SANK-shun · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To sanction to formally approve or authorize something, or to formally punish or penalize something -- a word with two nearly opposite meanings, depending on context.

The international committee voted to sanction the country's Olympic team, banning it from the next three competitions.

Worked Example

The board voted to formally sanction the merger, giving their official blessing for the two companies to combine.

Sanction is one of the rare English words with two nearly opposite meanings: it can mean to formally approve or permit something (as here), or to formally punish or penalize something (as in economic sanctions against a country). Always check the context to know which sense is meant.

How Sanction Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

penalize

penalize: to formally punish someone for breaking a rule

authorize

authorize: to formally approve or give official permission for something

Antonyms

pardon

pardon: to forgive or excuse someone for an offense -- opposite of formally punishing

forbid

forbid: to formally refuse to allow something -- opposite of formally approving

How Strong Is It? — warn → sanction → blacklist

warn vs. sanction

warn vs. sanction: To warn is to caution someone about a possible negative consequence, without yet punishing them.

blacklist vs. sanction

blacklist vs. sanction: To blacklist is to formally exclude or ban someone from a group or activity as punishment, an even harsher step than a single sanction.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sanct-

root — sanct-: sacred, holy (Latin sanctus)

suffix — -ion

suffix — -ion: the act, process, or result of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Sanction comes from Latin sanctus ('sacred, holy') -- the same root behind the everyday word sacred. Something 'sanctioned' was originally something made sacred or officially binding by decree, which is how the word came to mean both formal approval and formal, binding punishment.
